text: People think the hotel sleeps. It does not. Around three in the morning the day is closed and a new one is opened, and that is when everything gets found out. Cards are charged overnight, so if a card is declined, it is declined at three fifteen and there is nobody awake to tell. Rooms that were marked clean but were never actually entered show up on my screen in red. A rate that was typed wrong twelve hours ago is corrected by me, quietly, and the guest never hears about it. That is most of the job, honestly. Fixing the day before anybody wakes up and finds out it was broken. The part nobody believes is the wake-up calls. They are automated now, all of them, except mine. I still make about nine a night by hand, because nine people every night do not trust a machine to wake them up for a flight, and I have never once thought they were wrong.

Twenty-two years on this floor, and I will tell you the thing nobody believes. Bags are almost never lost. They are delayed, and there is a difference. Here is what actually happens. You get an hour and ten minutes to change planes. Your bag gets about thirty-five, because it has to come off, be sorted, be read by a scanner and be driven across two miles of airport by somebody like me. Nothing is done by hand anymore except the driving. The tag is everything. If the tag is torn, if it is folded over the code, if it is wrapped around a handle the wrong way, the bag is pulled out of the line and it is handled by a person, and a person is slower than a machine. That is your delay right there. So when people ask me what they should do, I say one thing. Take the old tags off. Every single one. I have seen a bag sent to a city the owner visited three years ago, because the old tag was the one the scanner read first.
